blocks.text: Many endocrine glands of the body are controlled by the master gland i.e., pituitary gland. However, the master gland is itself controlled by a part of the brain i.e., hypothalamus. Hypothalamus contains special neurosecretory cells, which not only conduct nerve impulses but also secrete hormones.

Two hormones i.e., oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone (ADH) are made by neurosecretory cells of hypothalamus. The axons of neurosecretory cells transport oxytocin and ADH to the posterior pituitary, where they are stored for eventual release into blood.

Blood vessels connect hypothalamus with the anterior pituitary. Neurosecretory cells of hypothalamus secrete hormones that travel to the anterior pituitary through these blood vessels. These hormones are of two kinds

blocks.alt: Section of the hypothalamus and pituitary. Neurosecretory cells (orange stars) lie in the hypothalamus. Axons of most run down the stalk into the posterior pituitary; a few end at a capillary bed at the top of the stalk. An artery feeds that capillary bed and the anterior pituitary; a portal vessel runs from the stalk capillaries to capillaries in the anterior pituitary. Another artery enters the posterior pituitary; veins from both lobes join below.
blocks.caption: Figure 16.2: Hypothalamus and pituitary (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 16.2).

items: Releasing hormones stimulate the anterior pituitary to make and secrete hormones.
Inhibiting hormones inhibit production and secretion of anterior pituitary hormones.
